Use case: stylized-concept. Low-poly concept art for THESEUS, an inhabited human-only space trading game. A coherent world of uneven human technological development and objects with biographies: early atomic-age optimism, heavy 1950s American automobile manufacturing, prewar eastern-European civic/market materials, later sophisticated technology fitted into inherited machinery. No aliens, no fantasy races. NOT a random steampunk costume collage. NO gratuitous gears, neon cyberpunk, holographic screens, gas-mask fetish, war propaganda, corporate logos or flags. Construction logic and worn useful objects explain the mixture. Delightful primitive pseudo-3D, crisp orthographic/isometric composition, visible 8–12-sided cylinders and faceted solids, broad plain matte material faces with a few semigloss enamel or chrome bands. Wear expressed through sparse geometric chips, patches and slightly mismatched panels, not grunge textures or realistic scratches. Simple warm directional light, cool lavender shadow, clear separation of shapes. Modest browser-game-feasible visual complexity, intentionally chunky, NOT a photoreal or cinematic render, not a high-detail film prop. Color language: petrol teal, warm ivory, faded oxblood, ochre, charcoal, brass accents and muted violet space. Slightly used, cared for, sometimes absurd, never cute-faced. All tiny labels lowercase and sparse. These are world concept illustrations, not dashboards or dense UI mockups.
Landscape paired ship study, TWO fully visible large spacecraft on a plain dark plum background, same three-quarter orthographic camera. Title "theseus / second lives".
LEFT: "the sunday catch" — an affluent trader's restored former orbital fishing / ice-harvesting vessel, now a unique luxury yacht. Keep an awkward broad blunt utility hull, deep working belly, two original chunky winch drums, folded retrieval booms, an old reinforced cargo hatch, large old-fashioned octagonal stern engine housings. The owner has added beautifully maintained petrol-teal and warm-ivory enamel panels, restrained thick chrome waist bands, one glazed panoramic salon inserted into the old wheelhouse, a small sheltered observation terrace occupying the former work deck, a tiny preserved fish emblem near the old registry plate. One modern compact ceramic-white navigation module and modern drive inserts visibly sit within inherited housings. It is a spacecraft, no water, no ship's sails, no yacht ocean bow. Its ungainly original industrial silhouette survives the expensive restoration. Simple enough to model from 50–80 solid shapes.
RIGHT: "last tram to sol" — a working family-owned interplanetary courier derived from heavy 1955 American luxury-car proportions: rounded blunt cabin, huge split wraparound window, broad ribbed service grille that functions as a heat exchanger, cream and faded burgundy enamel, small brass handles, two long shoulder pods resembling fenders but enclosing cylindrical propellant tanks. Short fin-shaped radiator slabs have an obvious functional purpose. A small modern jade nav sensor and recently replaced gray engine pod contrast with lovingly repaired old bodywork. A few strapped delivery crates below the centerline, one mismatched access panel. NO wheels, NO literal car floating in space, NO aircraft wings. It is an original spacecraft with the visual vocabulary of a power cruiser.
Both ships should feel human, distinct, inviting and buildable in primitive low-poly geometry. Generous space between them, small names beneath, no inset detail overload, no platform.

Landscape isometric scene "theseus / the exchange". A compact, inviting indoor space-station market with 1930s eastern-European covered-market construction vocabulary: cream ceramic tile at the base of stout oxblood iron columns, timber service counters, muted green enamel stall signs, a high simple ribbed steel roof cropped away for dollhouse visibility. Market merchants and customers are tiny faceless blocky HUMAN figures wearing varied ordinary work clothes. No extravagant costumes.
Foreground merchant counter has a chunky brass mechanical balance scale, three visually distinct goods in simple geometry: ochre ore chunks in a wooden crate, sage grain sacks, a blue-gray box of machine parts. A handwritten price slate, stamped paper manifests, and a modest new flat navigation/payment terminal bolted to the worn wooden counter. Beside a kettle stands a compact atomic-age cream-and-teal appliance with a tiny atom emblem and plain amber status lamp, not a glowing reactor. It is a matter-of-fact household object. One stall immaculate and recently painted, another repaired with different timber: different owners, shared building traditions.
Through a broad rear loading opening, a partial silhouette of a restored teal and ivory spacecraft is visible against muted violet space, with an enclosed cargo transfer collar establishing the pressurized station setting. No open human exposure to vacuum. Stack several simple crates near the airlock, a small old wheeled freight trolley, a tidy rope reel. Warm pendant lamps, one cooler replacement strip lamp. Limited props, legible architecture, plain low-poly shapes, charming everyday business, not a dystopian bazaar, not ornate nostalgia scenery. Main action two humans choosing goods across the scale. Minimal signs "exchange", "grain", "parts". No UI.

Landscape exterior isometric space-station concept, title "theseus / port of many hands". A modest inhabited trading station floating against quiet dark aubergine space, full structure visible and built from 70–100 clear chunky geometric forms, not an enormous megacity. The station has a coherent old central core resembling early atomic-era industrial civic architecture translated to vacuum: squat cream pressure drums, ribbed oxblood steel frames, broad green-enamel docking signs, thick glazed observation bands and a simple central communications mast.
Visible history through additions: one beautifully restored cream-and-teal passenger berth with chrome bands; one battered ochre freight gantry and bulky storage tanks; a newer austere white research module docked to a practical adapter; old cylindrical habitations joined by thick enclosed access tunnels. Exposed small radiator slabs and a few simple communications dishes are clearly equipment, not decoration. No atmosphere, no clouds, no ocean, no ground, no open-air pedestrian plazas. Any greenery is inside a tiny visibly sealed greenhouse. Different construction eras share pressure collars and utility routes.
At most TWO small docked ships: a refurbished broad old working vessel now painted like a luxury cruiser, and a plain utilitarian cargo tug. One small tender approaching. These support scale and human variety, not visual clutter. Warm windows sparse, signs very few and lowercase, e.g. "arrivals", "freight". Strong readable silhouette and large negative spaces between modules. Each addition plausible as a repair or expansion, with a few mismatched panel colors. Friendly commerce frontier rather than military fortress. Low-poly simple forms and flat color areas are essential.

Landscape isometric dollhouse interior, title "theseus / signals office". A small inviting space-station communications office combining a prewar eastern-European post-office counter with early atomic-age equipment and one genuinely modern communication device. It must feel like normal people sending messages over extraordinary distances.
Room has cream lower wall tiles, petrol-teal metal equipment cabinets, dark timber counter with a small brass service grille, worn muted oxblood floor slabs and a broad sealed porthole showing a sliver of violet space. Main console is a low-poly cream-enamel instrument desk with large physical knobs, a chunky telephone handset, TWO small green monochrome screens and one modern thin dark display inserted into a plainly mismatched adapter frame. A little receipt printer ejects a pale paper strip. NO giant luminous screen wall or holograms. A freestanding simple white ceramic-and-brass ansible transceiver canister sits behind glass as a precious imported component connected to the old switchboard by one thick visible conduit.
One seated blocky human operator, one standing traveler holding a folded letter and one tiny luggage case. Human-only, no robots or aliens needed. Small signs "local", "long distance", "signals"; one small screen legibly says "arrival: 14 min" to suggest delayed messages. A pinned paper route diagram and pigeonholes for printed messages, only a few envelopes. One warm task lamp, cool fill at the window. This is a quiet social service space with technology from several generations, not a cockpit or spy bunker. Simple readable solids, broad untextured color planes, limited details, affectionate everyday atmosphere. No UI overlay.
